title: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate · Units 35–36

units.title: Unit 35 — Jobs
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 76–77 (PDF pages 77–78).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Occupations, job duties and public services
learningObjectives: Name practical trades and professional occupations and explain what workers do.
Distinguish repair, fix and mend in contexts involving equipment, buildings and clothes.
Talk about medical workers, including GPs, dentists, vets, nurses and surgeons, with accurate verb patterns.
Identify jobs in the armed forces and emergency services and use join the army, navy, air force, police force and fire brigade.
Connect occupations to their materials, workplaces and activities.

items.example: A builder repaired the wall behind our house.
items.note: Someone who builds or repairs buildings, especially homes.

items.example: The carpenter made some shelves for the office.
items.note: A person who makes or repairs things using wood.

items.example: We called a plumber when a pipe started leaking.
items.note: A worker who installs and repairs water pipes and plumbing.

items.example: An electrician checked the wiring before we moved in.
items.note: A worker who installs or repairs electrical systems and equipment.

items.example: The mechanic found the problem with my car.
items.note: A person who repairs machines, especially cars.

items.example: The builder used bricks to repair the garden wall.
items.note: Building material identified in the unit's job illustration.

items.example: She chose strong wood for the new table.
items.note: The material a carpenter commonly works with.

items.example: Water was leaking from a pipe in the kitchen.
items.note: A hollow tube that carries water or other substances.

items.example: The electrician replaced a broken wall socket.
items.note: A point where a plug is connected to the electricity supply.

items.example: They repaired the roof after the storm.
items.note: Repair means make a damaged or broken thing work or become good again.

items.example: Can you fix this broken chair?
items.note: In this sense fix and repair have similar meanings; fix is also common in everyday speech.

items.example: My grandmother mended the hole in my jacket.
items.note: Common with clothes and sometimes small items; compare fix and repair.

items.pt: remendar roupas; consertar peças de roupa
items.example: He learnt to mend clothes instead of throwing them away.
items.note: Mend is particularly natural with clothes and fabric.

items.example: The delivery company replaced the damaged equipment.
items.note: Damaged things may still work but need repair; compare broken.

items.example: The printer is broken, so we cannot print the forms.
items.note: A broken thing may be physically damaged or no longer work.

items.example: Medicine is a profession that requires years of training.
items.note: The source uses professions for jobs requiring substantial education or training.

items.example: An architect designed the new community centre.
items.note: An architect designs buildings.

items.example: She wants to design buildings that use less energy.
items.note: Design means plan the form and details of something.

items.example: The lawyer explained the contract to her client.
items.note: A lawyer helps or represents people with legal problems.

items.example: Lawyers represent people during legal disputes.
items.note: Represent means act or speak on someone else's behalf.

items.example: They asked a lawyer for help with a legal problem.
items.note: A difficulty or issue involving the law.

items.example: An engineer designed a safer bridge.
items.note: In the textbook's example, engineers plan roads, bridges, machines and similar structures.

items.example: Our accountant prepared the company's financial report.
items.note: Someone who works with financial accounts for people or organisations.

items.example: An accountant can explain a company's financial situation.
items.note: Financial describes matters involving money and accounts.

items.example: The university lecturer teaches first-year engineering students.
items.note: A university teacher; in British English not all lecturers have the title Professor.

items.pt: ministrar aula expositiva; dar uma palestra acadêmica
items.example: She gives a lecture on energy systems every Monday.
items.note: A typical activity of a university lecturer.

items.example: Several people in his family work in the medical profession.
items.note: A collective expression for doctors and related medical professionals.

items.example: The doctor treats patients with a range of health problems.
items.note: Treat someone means give medical care or assistance.

items.pt: clínico geral; médico de atenção primária (Reino Unido)
items.example: She booked an appointment with her GP.
items.note: British abbreviation for general practitioner, a doctor who usually works outside hospital.

items.pt: médico de clínica geral; médico generalista
items.example: A general practitioner can refer you to a specialist.
items.note: Full form of GP in British healthcare usage.

items.example: I visit the dentist twice a year.
items.note: A professional who looks after people's teeth.

items.example: The vet examined our cat after it stopped eating.
items.note: Common shortened form of veterinary surgeon, who treats animals.

items.pt: consultório; clínica médica ou veterinária (Reino Unido)
items.example: The GP's surgery is next to the pharmacy.
items.note: In this context surgery is a doctor's or vet's workplace; it can also mean an operation.

items.example: The nurse checked the patient's temperature.
items.note: A healthcare worker who helps care for patients.

items.example: Nurses look after patients on the ward.
items.note: Look after means take care of someone; it is not the same as merely looking at them.

items.example: The surgeon explained the operation to the family.
items.note: A doctor who performs medical operations.

items.pt: operar alguém; realizar cirurgia em alguém
items.example: The surgeon operated on the patient yesterday.
items.note: Use the preposition on when referring to the person receiving surgery.

items.example: They requested medical help after the accident.
items.note: Help provided by health professionals; associated with treat in the source.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: She considered a career in the armed forces.
items.note: A collective term for a country's military services.

items.pt: entrar para o Exército; alistar-se no Exército
items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: My cousin joined the army after leaving school.
items.note: Join means become a member of an organisation or service.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The soldier completed his training last month.
items.note: A person serving in the army.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: Her brother serves in the navy.
items.note: The branch of the armed forces that operates at sea.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: He joined the navy when he was nineteen.
items.note: Join the navy is the natural construction for becoming a sailor in the military.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The sailor spent several months at sea.
items.note: Here a sailor is associated with naval service; sailor can also describe a civilian.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: His sister works in the air force.
items.note: The military service that operates aircraft.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: She joined the air force after university.
items.note: A natural expression for becoming a member of the air force.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The pilot landed the aircraft safely.
items.note: In the unit's illustration, the pilot belongs to the air force.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The fighter pilot trained to fly a military aircraft.
items.note: A pilot trained to fly fighter aircraft; introduced by the exercises.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: A police officer helped us find the station.
items.note: A person working in the police service.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: He has worked in the police force for ten years.
items.note: The police service as an organisation.

items.pt: ingressar na polícia; entrar para a corporação policial
items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: She joined the police force after completing her training.
items.note: Use join with the name of the service, not become a police force.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The firefighter rescued a family from the building.
items.note: Gender-neutral occupation term; the text also gives fireman.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: He trained as a fireman many years ago.
items.note: Traditional masculine term; firefighter is the more inclusive modern term.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The fire brigade arrived within a few minutes.
items.note: British English name for the fire service.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: He joined the fire brigade after training as a firefighter.
items.note: Use this pattern for becoming part of the service.

items.section: D · Armed forces and emergency services
items.example: The emergency services responded to the road accident.
items.note: The organisations that respond to emergencies, such as fire and police services.

units.title: Unit 36 — Talking about your work
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 78–79 (PDF pages 79–80).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Pre-intermediate and Intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: Workplace communication, duties, pay and conditions
learningObjectives: Ask and answer common questions about occupations, employers and industries.
Explain professional duties using set up, deal with, handle, run, advise, involve, in charge of and responsible for.
Use work and advice as uncountable nouns, and distinguish advise from advice.
Distinguish salary, wages, income, earning and income tax.
Describe fixed hours, overtime, the working day, working conditions, time off and the minimum wage.

items.pt: Com o que você trabalha?; Qual é sua profissão?
items.example: What do you do, and how long have you worked there?
items.note: In this context the question asks about someone's occupation, not an activity they are doing now.

items.word: What do you do for a living?
items.pt: O que você faz para ganhar a vida?
items.ipa: /wɒt də juː duː fər ə ˈlɪvɪŋ/
items.example: What do you do for a living, if you don't mind me asking?
items.note: A question specifically about someone's job or source of livelihood.

items.pt: Qual é seu trabalho?; Qual é sua profissão?
items.example: What's your job at the new company?
items.note: A direct question about someone's work; more direct than What do you do?

items.example: I work in marketing for a technology company.
items.note: Work in is often followed by a field, industry or department.

items.example: She works in sales and speaks to clients every day.
items.note: Sales is the activity or department that sells products or services.

items.pt: trabalhar para uma empresa; ser empregado de uma empresa
items.example: He works for a small engineering company.
items.note: Work for identifies the employer; work in typically identifies the field.

items.example: My sister works as a hairdresser in the town centre.
items.note: A person who cuts and styles people's hair.

items.example: The sales department is hiring new staff.
items.note: In this context sales refers to selling goods or services.

items.example: She manages online marketing for the firm.
items.note: Activities used to promote and sell products or services.

items.example: The business consultant helped them plan their new service.
items.note: Someone who gives specialist advice to organisations or businesses.

items.example: A consultant reviewed the company's marketing plan.
items.note: A specialist who advises others in a particular area.

items.example: We advise clients on choosing reliable equipment.
items.note: Verb spelled with s and ending in a voiced z sound; compare the noun advice.

items.example: She gave me useful advice about the interview.
items.note: Uncountable noun spelled with c; say some advice or a piece of advice, not an advice.

items.example: The financial adviser gives advice to first-time buyers.
items.note: Advice is a noun after give; do not write give advise.

items.pt: abrir uma empresa; montar um negócio
items.example: They plan to set up a business after finishing university.
items.note: Set up here means start and organise a new business.

items.pt: lidar com algo; cuidar de um assunto
items.example: I deal with customer questions every morning.
items.note: Deal with describes handling tasks, people or situations.

items.example: Our support team deals with complaints promptly.
items.note: A common workplace collocation, highlighted by the exercise text.

items.example: She handles difficult customer enquiries calmly.
items.note: Here handle is a verb meaning manage or deal with, not a physical handle.

items.example: I'm responsible for maintaining the test equipment.
items.note: Use responsible for + noun or -ing form.

items.pt: estar encarregado de; estar à frente de
items.example: He is in charge of a team of six technicians.
items.note: To have authority or control over something or someone.

items.example: The company is developing a new product for schools.
items.note: Something that a business makes or provides to sell.

items.pt: administrar uma empresa; gerir um negócio
items.example: She runs a small business with her brother.
items.note: Run here means organise and manage, not move quickly.

items.pt: gerir um departamento; chefiar um setor
items.example: He runs the customer service department.
items.note: Run in this sense means supervise or manage an organisational unit.

items.pt: diário; cotidiano; do dia a dia
items.example: She handles the day-to-day problems in the office.
items.note: Adjective before a noun for routine activities that happen every day.

items.pt: operações cotidianas; atividades diárias do negócio
items.example: The manager is responsible for the day-to-day business of the clinic.
items.note: Refers to the ordinary daily running of an organisation.

items.example: Our team meets briefly every Monday.
items.note: A group of people working together.

items.example: The receptionist booked an appointment for the customer.
items.note: A worker who welcomes visitors and answers calls.

items.pt: gerente de contas; responsável por contas
items.example: The accounts manager checked the clinic's bills.
items.note: In this source context, a person who manages financial accounts; titles vary between workplaces.

items.example: The secretary arranged an appointment with the director.
items.note: Someone who performs administrative and organisational tasks.

items.example: I spend Friday afternoons catching up on admin.
items.note: Informal shortened form of administration, referring to administrative work.

items.example: She works in administration at a local hospital.
items.note: Organising records, processes and other routine office tasks.

items.example: We ordered new equipment for the laboratory.
items.note: Normally uncountable; say some equipment or a piece of equipment.

items.example: The hotel received a complaint about the room.
items.note: A statement that something is wrong or unsatisfactory.

items.example: Several customers complained about the delay.
items.note: Verb corresponding to the noun complaint.

items.pt: fazer uma reclamação; apresentar uma queixa
items.example: He made a complaint about the late delivery.
items.note: The normal verb–noun collocation is make a complaint.

items.example: I have a lot of work to finish before Friday.
items.note: Work is generally uncountable when meaning tasks or effort; do not say many works in this sense.

items.pt: meu trabalho envolve; minhas atividades incluem
items.example: My job involves testing electronic equipment.
items.note: Involve takes a noun or -ing form, not to + infinitive in this sense.

items.example: The new position involves travelling between offices.
items.note: Use involves travelling, not involves to travel.

items.example: The consultant explained the proposal to her client.
items.note: Common for clients of professional services and advice; customer is broader.

items.example: Financial advisers advise clients about loans.
items.note: Advise is a verb; compare give advice to clients.

items.example: They spoke to a financial adviser before taking out a loan.
items.note: A specialist who advises people about financial matters; used in Exercise 36.4.

items.pt: financiamento imobiliário; empréstimo com garantia hipotecária
items.example: She took out a mortgage to buy her first flat.
items.note: A loan secured on a property; present in the exercise account of an adviser.

items.example: He specialises in small business accounting.
items.note: British spelling with s; generally followed by a noun or -ing form.

items.example: The company pays its staff at the end of the month.
items.note: Pay is the verb; paid is its past tense and past participle.

items.example: Her annual salary is paid in twelve monthly instalments.
items.note: In the textbook, salary is typically regular pay for office or professional work.

items.pt: salários; remuneração por hora, dia ou semana
items.example: The workers receive their wages every Friday.
items.note: Often refers to payment for hourly, daily or weekly work; compare salary.

items.example: Her income comes from two part-time jobs.
items.note: Income can include earnings from several jobs and other sources.

items.example: He earns more when he works extra hours.
items.note: Earn and make can refer to receiving money for work.

items.example: They hope their small business will make money.
items.note: A common informal expression for earning or obtaining money.

items.example: Income tax is deducted from part of her earnings.
items.note: A tax on income; actual tax rules vary by country.

items.example: Some of our taxes are paid to the government.
items.note: The source notes that part of income goes to the government as tax.

items.example: He prefers fixed hours because he collects his children from school.
items.note: Hours that remain the same rather than changing daily.

items.pt: emprego com horário comercial; trabalho das nove às cinco
items.example: She chose a nine-to-five job after years of shift work.
items.note: Conventional expression for a job with regular daytime office hours; not always literally 9 to 5.

items.pt: horas extras; trabalho além do expediente
items.example: There is a lot of overtime during busy periods.
items.note: Work done beyond usual working hours.

items.example: We sometimes work overtime to finish a project.
items.note: You can say do overtime or work overtime.

items.example: Staff get paid for overtime at the end of each month.
items.note: Not all workers receive additional pay for overtime.

items.example: Good working conditions help employees stay healthy.
items.note: The circumstances in which people do their jobs.

items.example: The contract includes paid holidays.
items.note: Time away from work during which employees continue to be paid.

items.example: I asked for time off to attend an appointment.
items.note: A period when someone is not working; it may be paid or unpaid.

items.example: The employer must respect the legal minimum wage.
items.note: The lowest wage permitted by applicable law; rates vary by place and time.

items.example: A regional manager oversees several local teams.
items.note: A workplace role introduced in the extended exercise.

items.example: I am in contact with suppliers throughout the week.
items.note: A common expression for regular communication with people.
